title: Racial atmosphere in Pontiac and the migration from the South
summary: Pontiac was placid when he lived there but polarized by the 1940s-50s; his father came north recruited for factory work.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: What was the racial atmosphere in Pontiac?

At the time, when I lived there, it was relatively placid. Later, it became polarized. Later meeting after I had left and then to come back. I ran into discrimination and segregation, which I didn't know I was living there. I ran into that on subsequent visits back to Pontiac, which was rather strange.
We’re talking about when I made trips back to Pontiac in the 40s. Yes the 40s or 50s. That is when the polarization took place.
Was this polarization rooted within conflicts within the workforce? Competition for jobs?

I suspect that that had something to do with it. More and more people would come up from the south looking for work, and maybe the work wasn't as plentiful in those days as it had been earlier. You see, when my father came, he came there as a result of people who had come through the South, or had made inquiries our head made excursions and visits down there to get workers to come north.
So, right after World War I, or during World War I in that industrial surge, your father was part of that first wave of migration patterns.

Exactly, and that continued for 20 years or more. The workers entered a saturation point. It became more workers then there were jobs. I guess I created a lot of tensions. I guess that resulted in the polarization, other factors may have been present. I'm not sure.
